articles.summary: There’s a puzzle facing the federal government after a routine wiring job at a remote FAA outpost stopped air travel nationwide Friday: If an old router grounded America, how do you replace the rest while the planes are still flying? Thousands of flights were canceled, and roughly 1.5 million travelers were thrown into chaos. Officials the decades-old equipment that caused the nightmare scenario won’t be the last to fail. “It’s going to continue to fail,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned. The fix is a slow piece-by-piece swap while the system stays running. So far, about 69% of the FAA’s copper phone lines have been switched to fiber. Crews have installed 224 digital voice switches, converted 469 radio sites, and added electronic flight strips at 25 towers where controllers still hand paper slips to each other. The first phase of the agency’s broader overhaul is supposed to wrap up by the end of 2028. Doing that work without disrupting traffic comes down mostly to timing.
